findings.claim: Every lesson (14 of 14) labels its comparison question "4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different" and closes the mark scheme "[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison]".
findings.truth: On this paper the thematic-study comparison question carries 8 marks, 4 for each way. A student practising it at half tariff writes half the answer the question needs. Type and mark-scheme tail corrected in all 14 lessons; a line was added noting that the exam sets either the similarity or the difference version, never both.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/history-8145-8145.md 4.4.2 Section A question table (Q1 8, Q2 8, Q3 8, Q4 16 + 4 SPaG = 40 + 4).

findings.claim: Every lesson sets two 8-mark questions typed "Explain a Development" ("Explain how ... developed") — 28 across the unit — and no lesson sets a source question at all.
findings.truth: Section A of this paper sets exactly four forms: source utility (8), significance (8), two ways similar/different (8) and the 16-mark factors essay. "Explain how..." belongs to the British depth study in Section B. All 28 were converted with rebuilt mark schemes: one per lesson to "How useful is Source A...?" using a real named source (zodiac-man almanac, John of Arderne's treatise, the 1348 Paris faculty report, Paré's own account, a Dr James's Powder advertisement, Gillray 1802, Koch's 1877 bacteria photograph, Lister in The Lancet 1867, Snow's 1855 map, Nightingale's 1858 diagram, Rowntree 1901, Fleming 1929, the BMA's January 1948 statement, the Beveridge Report), and one per lesson to an 8-mark significance question. Every lesson now practises all four real forms. No source was invented and none carries an archive provenance.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/history-8145-8145.md 4.4.2, Section A and Section B question tables.

findings.claim: All 14 factors essays use a quoted statement plus "To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer."
findings.truth: This paper's 16-mark question is a factors question in the form "Has X been the main factor in ...? Explain your answer with reference to X and other factors." The quoted-statement form belongs to other boards. All 14 stems reworded; the mark schemes already carry the correct 16 + 4 SPaG tariff.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/history-8145-8145.md 4.4.2, Q4 description; brief's stated stem.

findings.claim: Invented exam claims: "examiners reward students who explain that it was internally coherent" (L1), "Examiners reward students who acknowledge this gap" (L4), "demonstrates the 'over time' criterion examiners reward" (L5), "significant in three ways that examiners want students to bring out" (L6).
findings.truth: No published source says what examiners reward in these terms. Each rewritten as advice about what a strong answer does.
findings.evidence: House rule on invented exam claims; nothing in the spec supports the claims.

findings.claim: "The mark scheme rewards students who show religion as both helping and hindering" (L2), "The mark scheme rewards explicit comparison ... is what unlocks the top band" (L7), "The mark scheme rewards substantiated comparison" (L9).
findings.truth: These assert the contents of a board mark scheme. Rewritten as "the strongest answers ...", which keeps the teaching point and honours the copyright-distancing rule.

findings.claim: "Examiner reports flag every series that strong answers move fluently between periods" (garbled), "AQA principal examiner reports flag the same mistakes every series", and a flashcard asking "What examiner red flag describes writing in the first person?" answered "AQA reports flag this every series".
findings.truth: Invented examiner-report claims, one of them incoherent. All three rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: No examiner report is cited or citable; house rule on invented exam claims.

findings.claim: "banned routine dissection in 1163" (L2 key fact), "the same Church banned dissection in 1163" (L2 exam tip), and "banned by the Church in medieval Britain except in rare licensed cases" (L1 glossary and dfn).
findings.truth: The 1163 Council of Tours barred clergy from cutting open bodies; it did not ban dissection, which was carried on in Italian medical schools from the early 1300s. Both lessons' own body text says exactly this ("rare and tightly controlled"), so the summaries contradicted the articles they summarise.
findings.evidence: Lesson 2 content_html; Wikipedia 'Council of Tours' records no medical decree; the ban claim is not supported.

findings.claim: al-Razi "ran the first medical hospital in Baghdad" (dfn, glossary, flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Al-Razi directed a hospital at Rayy and then the Baghdad hospital founded under al-Mu'tadid, later building a larger one. Baghdad had hospitals before him. Changed to "the main hospital in Baghdad".

findings.claim: Bubonic plague caused "about a 60% mortality rate even with modern treatment".
findings.truth: Bubonic plague kills 30–60% of those infected when untreated; antibiotics cut that sharply and recovery is usual if treatment starts in time. Corrected in the article and on the flashcard.

findings.claim: "Compare this to Christchurch Priory, where 12th-century plans show piped water ..."
findings.truth: The famous 12th-century waterworks drawing is Christ Church Priory, Canterbury, not Christchurch Priory in Dorset. The lesson's own mark scheme says "Christchurch, Canterbury".
findings.evidence: Lesson 3 practice mark scheme; the Canterbury waterworks plan (Eadwine Psalter, c1160).

findings.claim: At Padua, Vesalius "dissected bodies himself, often using corpses he stole from a gibbet outside the city walls".
findings.truth: From 1539 a Padua criminal-court judge agreed to supply Vesalius with the bodies of executed criminals. The gibbet theft belongs to his student days, before Padua. Both facts kept, in the right order.

findings.claim: "Hunter taught Edward Jenner directly between 1764 and 1772."
findings.truth: Jenner was apprenticed to the Chipping Sodbury surgeon Daniel Ludlow from 1764 and only came to Hunter at St George's in 1770. Corrected to 1770–1772.

findings.claim: "George III's son Octavius died of it [smallpox] in 1783."
findings.truth: Octavius, aged four, died on 3 May 1783 a few days after being inoculated against smallpox. The cause was never settled and the royal household blamed a cold. Reworded to say he died days after inoculation.

findings.claim: "Jenner repeated the experiment on 23 more cases, including his own son, before publishing."
findings.truth: The 1798 Inquiry set out 23 case histories in total, with Phipps as case 17; his own 11-month-old son was among them. Reworded.

findings.claim: Inoculation defined as "giving someone a mild dose of smallpox by injecting pus from a smallpox patient" (dfn and glossary).
findings.truth: Inoculation was done by working pus into a scratch in the skin, as the lesson's own article says ("usually rubbed into a scratch on the arm"). Syringe injection is an anachronism here.

findings.claim: "Third, ordinary people who feared the new and risked nothing they could afford to lose."
findings.truth: The sentence says the opposite of what it means. Reworded to "feared something new and had nothing they could afford to risk".

findings.claim: "The French wine and silk industries hired him in the 1850s" and germ theory grew out of work "for the French brewing and silk industries".
findings.truth: Pasteur's fermentation work began in 1856; the silkworm disease work began in 1865, four years after the 1861 germ theory. The silk industry cannot have prompted a theory published before it hired him.

findings.claim: Rubber gloves "introduced by William Halsted in Baltimore in 1894 after his nurse's hands cracked from carbolic" (article, knowledge-check match option, flashcard and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: Halsted had Goodyear make rubber gloves for his scrub nurse Caroline Hampton in 1889; her dermatitis came from the theatre antiseptics. Date corrected in every field; the match mapping is unchanged.

findings.claim: "Snow mapped 578 deaths" (article and flashcard).
findings.truth: 616 people died in the Broad Street outbreak. 578 is not a figure in the record.

findings.claim: "She invented the polar-area chart" (article) and "What graphic did Nightingale invent ...?" (flashcard).
findings.truth: The polar-area diagram was used by André-Michel Guerry in 1829 and Léon Lalanne by 1830. Nightingale made it famous. Changed to "made the polar-area chart famous" and "use".

findings.claim: "one of the first women elected to the Royal Statistical Society in 1858".
findings.truth: She was the first female member, and the body was the Statistical Society of London until it became Royal in 1887.

findings.claim: "The Crimean War, beginning in 1854."
findings.truth: The Crimean War began in 1853; Britain declared war in March 1854 and Nightingale reached Scutari in November 1854.

findings.claim: The 1911 National Insurance Act gave "sick pay (10 shillings a week for 26 weeks)".
findings.truth: 10 shillings a week for the first 13 weeks, then 5 shillings a week for the next 13.

findings.claim: Glossary calls Charles Booth a "London ship-owner" while the article and flashcard call him a Liverpool ship-owner.
findings.truth: Booth was a Liverpool ship-owner who surveyed London. Glossary aligned with the article.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction; Booth's firm was Liverpool-based.

findings.claim: "Evacuation moved 1.5 million urban children to rural homes from September 1939."
findings.truth: The first wave moved about 1.5 million people: 826,950 unaccompanied schoolchildren, 523,670 mothers with young children and 12,705 pregnant women.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Evacuations of civilians in Britain during the Second World War'.

findings.claim: "In July 1945 the British electorate, while Churchill was still attending the Potsdam Conference, voted Labour into power ..."
findings.truth: Polling was on 5 July, twelve days before Potsdam opened on 17 July, and Churchill had returned to London for the count on 26 July. Clause removed.
findings.evidence: Standard chronology of the 1945 election and the Potsdam Conference.

findings.claim: "Hugh Gaitskell introduced prescription charges" (flashcard and a mark scheme), where the article correctly says charges for spectacles and false teeth.
findings.truth: The 1951 budget charged for dentures and spectacles; the shilling prescription charge came in 1952.

findings.claim: "The 1945 Labour landslide with a 145-seat majority ..."
findings.truth: Labour won 393 of 640 seats, a majority of 146.
findings.evidence: 1945 general election result (393 Labour, 197 Conservative), as given in the lesson itself.

findings.claim: Four flashcard answers are bare lists and fail the enumeration rule: "An unfavourable conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in 1345" (L3), "Fleming, Florey and Chain" (L12), "Want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness" (L13), "Science and technology — germ theory, antiseptics, vaccines and microbe identification" (L14).
findings.truth: All four rewritten to one idea per card. The L12 and L13 cards were re-pointed ("Which prize did they share?", "Which giant stood for poverty?") so the question still invites the answer given. Confirmed clean against scripts/_validate_content_json.py.

findings.claim: Description is 105 characters.
findings.truth: Descriptions must stay under 100 characters. Shortened to 92.

findings.claim: "At the Scutari military hospital in 1854 mortality was around 42% when Nightingale arrived; within six months it had fallen to roughly 2%" — repeated in a key fact, a knowledge check (the marked answer), a flashcard and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (a) The 42%→2% figures are the currency of GCSE textbooks and of the answers students are marked against, so leave them. (b) The causal framing is wrong: deaths at Scutari ROSE through Nightingale's first winter (4,077 died) and fell only after the government's Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers in March 1855; Nightingale herself never claimed credit for the fall. Recommendation: keep the figures, but change the framing in the article and key fact to say the fall came after the Sanitary Commission's work of spring 1855 alongside her regime of cleanliness — a two-field edit that leaves the knowledge check and flashcard answers untouched. I have not made this edit: it changes an answer students may be taught and is Tom's call.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Florence Nightingale' (Sanitary Commission March 1855; 4,077 deaths in the first winter; she never claimed credit).
findings.ruling: Figures kept; framing corrected in key fact, flashcard and mark scheme (Sanitary Commission March 1855 alongside her regime). KC answer untouched.

findings.claim: "In 1163 the Council of Tours banned clergy from cutting open bodies (the famous 'Ecclesia abhorret a sanguine' — the Church abhors blood)."
findings.truth: The attribution of that phrase to the 1163 council is disputed; historians of canon law hold it to be a much later coinage. The council's surviving canons deal with simony and heresy. The claim is standard in GCSE textbooks, so I have left it, but it is not safe to teach as a quotation from the council.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Council of Tours' lists no medical decree; no primary text found.

findings.claim: "Westminster Hospital opened in 1719, Guy's in 1724, the London in 1740"; the key fact and a match set call 1724 the year Guy's was founded.
findings.truth: Guy's was founded (endowed) by Thomas Guy in 1721 and took its first patients in 1724–25. The article's "opened ... in 1724" is defensible; the key fact's "founded ... (1724)" is not, strictly. Left alone because both dates are in textbook use and the ripple touches five fields.

findings.claim: PC Albert Alexander was "dying of sepsis after scratching his face on a rose thorn".
findings.truth: The rose-thorn detail is the traditional account and is disputed — his daughter said the injury came from a bombing raid. The date (February 1941) and the outcome are right. Left as the textbook account.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Albert Alexander (police officer)' notes the dispute.

findings.claim: "Penguin produced a cheap paperback" of the Beveridge Report (also asserted on a flashcard).
findings.truth: Could not be verified. The report was an HMSO publication and HMSO issued a cheap abridged edition. If the Penguin claim cannot be sourced it should become "a cheap abridged edition" in both places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Beveridge Report' records the printer but no Penguin edition.

findings.claim: "8.5 million pairs of glasses dispensed in the first year."
findings.truth: Not verifiable from the sources available. The figure most often quoted for the NHS's first year is 5.25 million pairs of spectacles, with 8.5 million usually attached to dental treatments — the two may have been conflated. Worth a check against an NHS history source before it stands.
findings.evidence: nhs.uk history page returned 404; Wikipedia 'History of the National Health Service' gives no first-year figures.

findings.claim: Inoculation cost "around £5 per child — a labourer's monthly wage"; and "The 1853 Vaccination Act ... sparking riots in towns including Leicester".
findings.truth: £5 was nearer two to three months' wages for an 18th-century labourer, so the comparison understates the barrier. Riots did follow the 1853 Act, but Leicester's mass anti-vaccination movement belongs to the 1870s and 1880s, not to 1853. Neither is mark-affecting on its own.
findings.evidence: Standard wage estimates; the Leicester movement's own chronology.

findings.claim: Vesalius described as a "Belgian anatomist" in the article, glossary and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Belgium did not exist until 1830; he was born in Brussels in the Habsburg Netherlands and is usually called Flemish or Brussels-born. The usage is normal in GCSE textbooks, so left alone.

findings.claim: "Plastic surgery began with Harold Gillies treating facial injuries at the Queen's Hospital, Sidcup."
findings.truth: Reconstructive surgery long predates Gillies; he founded modern plastic surgery. "Modern plastic surgery began ..." would be exact.

findings.claim: The 16-mark practice essays are scoped to one lesson's period ("in medieval Britain", "during the Renaissance", "in the germ theory revolution").
findings.truth: The real 16-mark question targets all four parts of the specified content, so it always spans c1000 to the present. The lesson-scoped essays are a deliberate practice reduction and the mark schemes do reach across periods, but a student should meet at least one whole-sweep essay per unit. Worth adding when the unit is next touched.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/history-8145-8145.md 4.4.2: "The question will target all four parts of the specified content."

findings.claim: "The plague returned repeatedly — over 30 outbreaks before the Great Plague of 1665."
findings.truth: Plague did return many times between 1348 and 1665, but the count of "over 30" could not be sourced. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: No source found for the count.

summary: Every lesson was sound on the substance the spec names — the dates, figures and people in the articles were overwhelmingly right — but the exam furniture was not: all 14 lessons under-priced the comparison question at 4 marks, all 14 set two 8-mark 'Explain a Development' questions that belong to the other section of this paper, none set a source question, and all 14 factors essays used another board's stem. Those were converted with rebuilt mark schemes and real named sources. Alongside them, 21 factual corrections (Halsted's gloves 1889 not 1894, Snow's 616 deaths not 578, Hunter taught Jenner from 1770 not 1764, plague mortality untreated not 'even with modern treatment', 1911 sick pay 13 + 13 weeks not 26, Vesalius's Padua corpses, Octavius's death, the 1939 evacuation figures, the Potsdam clause) and nine invented examiner or mark-scheme claims. 180 edits in all; one ADJUDICATE (the Scutari 42%-to-2% causal framing) and ten NOTEs.
